I went to see this 3 nights ago here in Cork, Ireland. It was the world premiere of it, in the  cinema in the Triskel Arts Centre as part of the Cork  Festival. I found "Strange Fruit" to be an excellent movie. It is a bit rough around the edges, but for a low-budget movie that is to be expected! In general the acting (particularly from the main lead Kent ) is , the cinematography and direction excellent, and the script hugely entertaining and thought-provoking, with some nice set-ups and witty dialogue. The ending was a bit sudden, with no conclusion given to characters and events once the finale came to its gripping end ... but perhaps that's what the filmmakers were going for? It certainly did make the movie more . I did like the fact that the main character never came to terms with his  on screen: it leaves you wondering whether or not he ever will, as in real-life sometimes these things are never settled. This was a good choice, to leave it unresolved rather than sentimentally wrapping it up!  and suspenseful throughout, "Strange Fruit" is a hugely ambitious debut and I have high hopes for what the writer/director Kyle Schickner will  next. He - and his colleagues - are a talent worth watching. I hope "Strange " gets a wider release , as more people deserve to see this movie, an above-average thriller with some original and insightful twists on homophobia and racism in America's Deep .  Recommended: 7/10

Based on the comments  so far, everyone seems to either  this movie or love it. I think it would be fair to point out that although this is not a GREAT movie, it has its interesting moments. For one thing, it was filmed on location in Colorado (was it  or Telluride? I can't remember, but it is in the credits). The  is absolutely stunning and spectacular. It's beautiful, even to me who lived in Colorado for several years. Next, it has Disney's penchant for wonderful character actors. Harry Morgan has never been in better form  when he plays in a Disney movie. He is literally hysterical. Also, remember the wonderful Mary Wickes? Although she has a "bit part" in  , she is great, as always. If you don't know who she is, think of the animated Disney  of Hunchback from Notre  (she was one of the gargoyles), and she was also the most interesting nun in "Sister Act", as well as the best nun in "The Trouble With Angels." She has always been a  character actress and most character actors never receive the recognition they deserve. In addition to character actors and all- casts, in the 1960s-1970s Disney may have not had the "greatest" movies, but, if you really watch some of them from beginning to end, you will NOTICE that every movie has some really funny or hysterical moment in it. The entire movie may not be funny, but there is always a comic gem (at least 1 or 2) in every single "live-action" movie Disney ever made. Whether it's Harry Morgan in one of his bellowing tones of voice, or Tim Conway  around, or Joe Flynn giving one of his priceless looks of horror, it is all good. The whole film may not be good, but there are ALWAYS hysterical moments in every Disney  from this period  I have ever seen. Disney in this time period  managed to make a person smile, despite the dumbness of the film. Bsed on  , I disagree with viewers who say every Disney movie in this  period is awful. That statement it not quite accurate. Rather, it is easier for me to give credit to the funny moments and  the weaknesses in the plots. Some live-action Disney  are true classics (Old Yeller, Bedknobs and , Mary Poppins), but for those that aren't, I am able to appreciate them for what they were -- good clean family fun in a time when movies had become vulgar, crude and offensive.

The 80's is largely considered the decade in which  decided to have fun. , there were some definite brains  it all ("Evil Dead II", "Night of the Creeps" and "Return of the Living Dead" for example) and then there were those movies that were mindless but had a definite low rent charm and were perfect for a night  beer and friends. Movies like "Pieces" and "Blood Diner" stacked rental shelves in the 80's and 90's, offering little in intelligence or craftsmanship but plenty in dumb entertainment. Kevin Tenney's 1988 movie "Night of the Demons" is a part of this tradition-stupid, poorly acted and not an original bone in it's body, but dammit if you don't have a good . The plot is so simplistic it just had to come from the 80's: a  of dumb teens played by a bunch of actors in their mid to late 20's decide to go to a party at Hull House thrown by Angela (Mimi Kinkade) and Suzanne (Scream Queen legend Linnea Quigley.) Well,  and co. decide to throw a séance. This turns out to be as Will Arnett's "Arrested Development" character Gob would call it, a "Huge Mistake," because a demonic force soon possesses Angela, and starts to get to the  as well. Take "The Evil Dead", "A  on Elm " and your average dumb dead teen flick, throw them in a blender, and " of the Demons" is what you get. The movie is anything but , and really, it's not a  movie. The whole thing is insanely derivative, the acting is terrible, the jokes often fall flat, the characters are annoying (especially the character of Stooge) and the plot  are numerous. That out of the way, it's still a lot of fun. So why? Well for one thing, the make up and gore effects are top notch,   really memorable moments (especially a nasty and  plane odd bit with a tube of lipstick) that really stick out. It also rarely if ever takes itself too seriously, yet with the exception of some terrible puns, plays it straight and never  the audiences time with winking self awareness. Plus, there's a definite energy and enthusiasm to the whole enterprise that's almost impossible to resist. Yeah, it's nothing special, but it knows that, and it couldn't be more  of that fact. It's a goofy party horror movie, and it never pretends to be  more. It  not be a classic, but "Night of the Demons" is a good example of horror  food done right. It might not be too memorable or original, but sometimes you don't want a fancy beer. Sometimes you want a Budweiser.
